decks.title: Introduction to Accounting, Part 1: Meaning, objectives, users and qualities
goals: Explain the meaning of accounting and distinguish it from book-keeping
State the objectives and roles of accounting
Identify internal and external users and what each needs
Describe reliability, relevance, understandability and comparability

slides.heading: What is accounting?
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **meaning** of accounting, its **objectives**, its **users** and the **qualities** of good information.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: meaning, objectives and role, users, and qualities of information
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every business, from a corner stall to a large company, needs to know how it is doing. Accounting gives the answer. In this part we learn what accounting means, why it is done, who reads its figures and what makes those figures worth trusting.

slides.heading: The meaning of accounting
slides.body_md: Accounting is a process of turning business events into financial information for decisions.

visual.caption: The accounting process, from identifying to communicating.

slides.narration: Accounting is a chain of eight stages. We identify events that can be shown in money, measure their value, record them, classify them under heads, summarise them into statements, analyse the figures, interpret what they mean and finally communicate the results to the people who need them.

slides.heading: Book-keeping and accounting

rows: Recording, summarising, analysing, interpreting and communicating
To keep complete and accurate data

visual.alt: Table comparing book-keeping and accounting by scope, purpose, skill needed and result

slides.narration: Book-keeping is the recording part of the work. It writes transactions in the books and sorts them under heads. Accounting is wider. It starts from the records, then summarises, analyses and interprets them, and explains the results to users. A clerk may do the book-keeping, but the accountant must understand the story behind the figures.

slides.heading: Branches of accounting

rows: Records the transactions of the whole business and reports its profit and financial position
Finds and analyses the cost of products, jobs and services
Presents information for planning, control and decisions

visual.alt: Table of the three branches of accounting: financial accounting for the whole business, cost accounting for the cost of products and management accounting for planning and control

slides.narration: Accounting has three main branches. Financial accounting records the whole business and reports its profit and financial position to outsiders. Cost accounting finds what it costs to make a product or perform a job. Management accounting presents information to managers so that they can plan, control and decide.

slides.heading: Quick check: order the process
slides.body_md: Arrange the stages of the accounting process in the right order.
slides.narration: Think about what must happen first before the figures can be summarised and explained.

slides.heading: Objectives of accounting

rows: Every transaction is written in an orderly way
Dhanpur Dairy notes each milk purchase and sale by date
Income of the period is compared with its expenses
The dairy compares a month of sales with a month of costs
Assets, liabilities and capital are shown on a date
The dairy lists what it owns and owes on 31 March
Figures reach those who must decide
The dairy gives its bank the year's statements

visual.alt: Table of the four objectives of accounting with meaning and an imagined dairy illustration

slides.narration: Accounting has four objectives. First, to keep a systematic record of every transaction. Second, to find the profit or loss of a period. Third, to show the financial position on a date, that is, what the firm owns and owes. Fourth, to give information to users. The table shows each with an imagined dairy.

slides.heading: Role of accounting

rows: Events become money terms and standard statements that many people can read
Past transactions are kept and can be looked up and verified
The statements show what the firm owns and owes now
Data is collected, processed and communicated
Each user gets the figures needed for a decision

visual.alt: Table of the five roles of accounting: language of business, historical record, current economic reality, information system and service to users

slides.narration: Accounting plays five roles. It is the language of business, because it turns events into standard money terms. It is a historical record. It shows current economic reality. It is an information system that collects, processes and communicates. And it serves each user with the figures that user needs.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which role?
slides.body_md: Match each statement about the imagined Meera Traders to the role of accounting it shows.

rows: Her one-page statement is read in the same way by her bank and her supplier
She looks up what she paid an electrician last June
On 31 March the statement shows goods worth ₹80,000 and creditors of ₹60,000
Data about bills is collected, sorted and reported to her banker

visual.alt: Worked example table matching four statements about Meera Traders to roles of accounting
visual.caption: Match each statement to a role.

slides.narration: Read each statement and ask what accounting is doing. A statement that her bank and supplier both read the same way shows the language of business. Looking up last June shows the historical record. The statement showing what she owns and owes today shows current economic reality. Sorting bills for the banker shows an information system.

visual.caption: Who uses accounting information.

slides.narration: Many people look at the same set of accounts. Inside the firm are the owners, the management and the employees. Outside it are banks and lenders, investors, suppliers and creditors, the government and tax authorities, consumers and researchers. Each of them uses the information for a different purpose.

slides.heading: Internal users and their needs

rows: Profit earned and the safety of the capital invested
Detailed facts to plan, control and decide
Ability to pay wages and bonus, and job security

visual.alt: Table of internal users, owners, management and employees, with what each wants from accounting information

slides.narration: Internal users work in or own the business. Owners want to know the profit and whether their capital is safe. Management needs detailed facts to plan, control and decide. Employees want to know whether the firm can pay wages and bonus and whether their jobs are secure.

slides.heading: External users and their needs

rows: Ability to pay interest and repay the loan
Return on money and risk of the investment
Ability to pay for goods bought on credit
Profit for tax and compliance with the law
Fairness of prices and continuity of supply

visual.alt: Table of external users, banks and lenders, investors, suppliers and creditors, government and tax authorities, consumers and researchers, with what each wants

slides.narration: External users deal with the firm from outside. A bank wants to be sure of repayment. An investor looks at return and risk. A supplier wants payment for goods sold on credit. Tax authorities need the profit. Consumers care about fair prices and supply, and researchers study the figures for trends.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the user
slides.body_md: Match each user of a tea company's accounts with what the user mainly wants.
slides.narration: Ask what decision each user must make.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: who needs what?
slides.body_md: Kaveri Bakery is an imagined firm in the imagined town of Dhanpur. Find who is asking and what is needed.

rows: Should a bank lend ₹1,50,000 for a new oven?
Should the flour supplier allow thirty days of credit?
Can the six bakers expect a bonus?
What profit is taxable this year?

visual.alt: Worked example table of questions at Kaveri Bakery with the user who asks and what the user needs
visual.caption: Find who asks and what is needed.

slides.narration: A bank deciding whether to lend rupees one lakh fifty thousand for an oven needs to know whether the bakery can repay. A flour supplier deciding on thirty days of credit needs to know whether dues are paid on time. The bakers want to know whether a bonus is possible. The tax officer needs the taxable profit.

slides.heading: Reliability

rows: Independent persons using the same evidence reach the same figure
Two checkers agree on a sales total from the bills
Bad debts are shown even though the owner would prefer not
A sale is shown at the price actually charged

visual.alt: Table of the three parts of reliability: verifiability, neutrality and faithful representation, with meaning and an imagined case

slides.narration: Good information must be reliable. That means it can be verified, so that independent persons using the same evidence reach the same figure. It must be neutral, free from bias. And it must be a faithful representation, describing what really happened and not what someone would like to see.

slides.heading: Relevance and understandability

rows: A weekly cost report reaches the baker before festival orders
Three years of rising sales help predict the next year
It confirms or corrects earlier expectations
Actual profit shows the forecast was too high
Users with reasonable knowledge can follow it

visual.alt: Table of relevance, with timeliness, predictive value and feedback value, and understandability, with meaning and an imagined case

slides.narration: Relevant information makes a difference to a decision. It must arrive in time, help users predict the future and confirm or correct earlier expectations. Understandable information is presented clearly enough for users with reasonable knowledge. A report no one can follow, or that comes too late, is of little use.

visual.caption: The four qualitative characteristics.

slides.narration: The fourth quality is comparability. Users should be able to compare a firm with itself over time, and with other firms. This needs the same methods year after year, with any change disclosed. The chart brings together reliability, relevance, understandability and comparability, with the parts of each.

slides.heading: Quick check: which quality?
slides.body_md: Two accountants examine the same bills and reach the same sales figure. Which quality does this show?
slides.narration: Think about independent persons using the same evidence.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: applying the qualities
slides.body_md: Say which quality of information fails in each imagined case.

rows: The owner of Pinewood Traders asks that bad debts be left out of the report
A cooperative report is full of technical terms its members cannot follow
Sunrise Garments changes its stock method every year without saying so
A cost report arrives after the order was already priced

visual.alt: Worked example table of four imagined cases and the quality of information each affects
visual.caption: Say which quality fails in each case.

slides.narration: Leaving out bad debts at the owner's request is a failure of neutrality. A report full of technical terms that members cannot follow fails understandability. Changing the stock method every year without saying so fails comparability. A cost report that arrives after the order was priced fails timeliness.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Identify, measure, record, classify, summarise, analyse, interpret, communicate
Records, profit or loss, financial position, information
Internal: owners, management, employees; external: lenders, investors, suppliers, government, consumers, researchers

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning, branches, objectives, users and qualitative characteristics

slides.narration: To sum up. Accounting identifies, measures, records, classifies, summarises, analyses, interprets and communicates financial information. It has three branches and four objectives. Its users are internal and external, each with its own needs. Good information is reliable, relevant, understandable and comparable.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1

rows: Book-keeping records; interpretation is part of accounting
Owners, management and employees are internal users
It covers verifiability, neutrality and faithful representation

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in Part 1 and what to write instead

slides.narration: Do not say that book-keeping includes interpretation. Remember that employees are internal users. When you write about reliability, name its three parts. In a definition, include the stages of the process. For a user question, name the user and say what that user wants.

slides.narration: Before we record a single entry we need a shared vocabulary. This part gives standard meanings for the terms that appear everywhere in accounting, each tied to an imagined business so you can see how it is used.

slides.heading: Entity and business transaction

rows: A person or organisation, with a separate existence for accounting, about which records are kept
An exchange of money or money's worth between the firm and another party, measurable in money
An event with no completed exchange of value
A customer asking the price of a pen

visual.alt: Table of entity and business transaction with meaning and an imagined example from Meera Traders

slides.narration: An entity is a person or organisation about which records are kept, with a separate existence for accounting. Meera Traders is an entity. A business transaction is an exchange of money or money's worth between the firm and another party, which can be measured in money. Selling pens for rupees five thousand in cash is one. A customer only asking a price is not.

slides.heading: Capital and drawings

rows: The amount the owner has put into the business, with profits left in it
Cash or goods the owner takes out for personal use

visual.alt: Table of capital and drawings with meaning and effect on the owner's claim

slides.narration: Capital is the amount the owner has put into the business, together with profits left in it. It is the owner's claim on the firm. Drawings are cash or goods which the owner takes out for personal use. Drawings reduce capital, and they are not an expense of the business.

visual.caption: How assets and liabilities are classified.

slides.narration: Assets and liabilities are each classified into non-current and current. Non-current assets last for many years and may be tangible, like land and machinery, or intangible, like patents and goodwill. Current assets turn into cash within a year. Liabilities due after twelve months are non-current. Those due within a year are current.

slides.heading: Liabilities

rows: Due after more than twelve months
A bank loan repayable in five years
Due within twelve months or the operating cycle

visual.alt: Table of non-current and current liabilities with meaning and examples

slides.narration: A liability is an amount the firm must pay to outsiders. A non-current liability is due after more than twelve months, for example a bank loan repayable in five years. A current liability is due within twelve months or the operating cycle, for example creditors and outstanding rent.

slides.heading: Assets

rows: Physical, held for use over many years
No physical form but of value, used over many years
Held for sale or to turn into cash within twelve months or the operating cycle

visual.alt: Table of non-current tangible, non-current intangible and current assets with meaning and examples

slides.narration: An asset is a resource owned by the firm that is expected to bring future benefit. A non-current tangible asset has physical form, like land. A non-current intangible asset has no physical form but value, like a patent. A current asset is held for sale or will turn into cash within twelve months, like stock and debtors.

slides.heading: Quick check: intangible or not?
slides.body_md: Which of the following is an intangible asset?
slides.narration: Think of the asset that has no physical form.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: capital of Meera Traders
slides.body_md: Meera Traders, an imagined stationery business in the imagined town of Ranipur, lists its balances. Find the capital.

visual.alt: Worked example table finding the capital of Meera Traders as total assets less total liabilities
visual.caption: Capital is the balancing figure.

slides.narration: Add the non-current assets, rupees five lakh fifty thousand, to the current assets, rupees two lakh twenty thousand. Total assets are rupees seven lakh seventy thousand. The liabilities, including the five year loan, come to rupees two lakh seventy thousand. Capital is assets minus liabilities, which is rupees five lakh.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: classify at the bakery
slides.body_md: Classify each item of the imagined Kaveri Bakery. Then find its capital.

rows: An oven bought for ₹90,000 and meant to serve for ten years
Rights to a recipe brand bought for ₹60,000
Flour and sugar lying in the store room, worth ₹25,000
A bank loan of ₹1,50,000 repayable after four years
Wages of ₹8,000 due to staff and payable next week
A hotel owes ₹12,000 for cakes bought on credit

visual.alt: Worked example table classifying seven items of Kaveri Bakery into assets and liabilities
visual.caption: Total assets ₹1,92,000, liabilities ₹1,58,000, so capital is ₹34,000.

slides.narration: An oven for ten years is a tangible non-current asset. A recipe brand is intangible. Flour in the store room, money due from the hotel and cash in the till are current assets. The loan due after four years is a non-current liability. Wages due next week are a current liability. Assets are rupees one lakh ninety two thousand, liabilities rupees one lakh fifty eight thousand, so capital is rupees thirty four thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: a loan
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason about a four-year bank loan are true.
slides.narration: Ask when the loan falls due.

slides.heading: Capital and revenue expenditure

rows: Spending that gives a benefit for more than one year or adds to an asset
Buying a delivery van; installing a machine
Spending whose benefit is used up in the current year

visual.alt: Table of capital and revenue expenditure with meaning and examples

slides.narration: Expenditure is spending by the business. If the benefit lasts for more than one year or adds to an asset, it is capital expenditure and it appears in the balance sheet. If the benefit is used up in the current year, it is revenue expenditure and it is charged to the profit and loss account. Installing a machine is capital. Repairs are revenue.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: capital or revenue?
slides.body_md: Kaveri Bakery makes six payments. Classify each.

rows: Painting the shop walls, done every year, ₹8,000
Paying ₹12,000 to install and fix a new mixing machine

visual.alt: Worked example table classifying six payments of Kaveri Bakery as capital or revenue expenditure

slides.narration: The van, the installation of the new machine and the display counter give lasting benefit, so they are capital expenditure, together rupees four lakh ninety seven thousand. Painting every year, oven repairs and flour for the month are revenue expenditure, together rupees forty one thousand.

slides.heading: Expense, income, profit, gain and loss

rows: Amount earned from the main activity or by way of gain, and credited to the owner's claim
Profit from incidental or occasional events
Selling an old computer of book value ₹12,000 for ₹15,000: ₹3,000
Fall in capital without benefit in return

visual.alt: Table of expense, income, profit, gain and loss with standard meanings and examples

slides.narration: An expense is a cost incurred in earning revenue. Income is what the business earns. Profit is the excess of income over expenses. A gain is a profit from an incidental event, such as selling an old computer for rupees fifteen thousand when its book value was rupees twelve thousand, which gives a gain of rupees three thousand. A loss is a fall in capital without any benefit in return.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: profit and capital
slides.body_md: Find the profit of Kaveri Bakery for the month, then roll the capital forward.

rows: Commission received from a tea stall
Less: Flour, sugar and butter used

visual.alt: Worked example table computing the profit of Kaveri Bakery as total income less total expenses
visual.caption: Profit is income less expenses.

slides.narration: Income is rupees one lakh eighty five thousand, made of sales and commission. Expenses are rupees one lakh forty five thousand. Profit is therefore rupees forty thousand. Adding profit to the opening capital and the new capital, and deducting drawings, gives the closing capital of rupees three lakh sixty five thousand.

slides.heading: Trade discount and cash discount

rows: Bulk buying or to a trader
Not recorded; only the net invoice amount
Recorded as discount allowed or received

visual.alt: Table comparing trade discount and cash discount by what they are allowed on, why, and treatment in the books

slides.narration: A discount is a deduction from a price. Trade discount is allowed on the list price, for example for buying in bulk, and is not recorded in the books, only the net invoice amount is. Cash discount is allowed on the invoice amount for payment within the agreed period, and it is recorded in the books.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a bill with two discounts
slides.body_md: Anand Sports, an imagined wholesaler, sells goods to a retailer. Find the amount paid.

headers: Anand Sports bill to a retailer (imagined)
rows: Less: cash discount at 2% for prompt payment

visual.alt: Worked example table of a bill from list price through trade discount, invoice amount and cash discount to the amount paid

slides.narration: The list price is rupees fifty thousand. Trade discount at ten per cent is rupees five thousand, so the invoice amount is rupees forty five thousand. Cash discount at two per cent of the invoice is rupees nine hundred. If the retailer pays within ten days, the amount actually paid is rupees forty four thousand one hundred.

slides.heading: Quick check: arrange the bill
slides.body_md: Arrange the steps of working out the amount paid on a bill with both discounts.
slides.narration: Cash discount is found on the invoice amount, not the list price.

slides.heading: Voucher, goods, purchases and sales

rows: Written evidence of a transaction, such as a cash memo or a receipt
Items the business buys for resale or manufacture and sells
Goods bought for resale or for use in production, cash or credit
Goods sent back to the supplier
Goods sent back by a customer

visual.alt: Table of voucher, goods, purchases, purchases return, sales and sales return with standard meanings

slides.narration: A voucher is written evidence of a transaction, such as a cash memo. Goods are items that the business buys to resell or to make into products. Purchases are goods bought, and purchases return is goods sent back to the supplier. Sales are goods sold, and sales return is goods sent back by a customer.

slides.heading: Stock, debtors and creditors

rows: Unsold goods at the start of the period
Unsold goods at the end of the period; the next period's opening stock
Persons who owe the firm for goods or services bought on credit
Persons the firm owes for goods or services bought on credit

visual.alt: Table of opening stock, closing stock, debtors and creditors with standard meanings and examples from Meera Traders

slides.narration: Opening stock is the unsold goods at the start of the period, and closing stock is the unsold goods at the end. Closing stock of one year becomes the opening stock of the next. A debtor is a person who owes the firm for goods bought on credit. A creditor is a person to whom the firm owes money for goods bought on credit.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: net purchases, net sales, debtor
slides.body_md: Compute net purchases and net sales for Meera Traders, and the balance due from Rohit Stationers.

visual.alt: Worked example table of net purchases and net sales of Meera Traders after deducting returns

slides.narration: Purchases of rupees one lakh fifty thousand less returns of rupees twelve thousand give net purchases of rupees one lakh thirty eight thousand. Sales of rupees two lakh forty thousand less returns of rupees fifteen thousand give net sales of rupees two lakh twenty five thousand. A customer who bought rupees eighteen thousand on credit and paid rupees six thousand is still a debtor for rupees twelve thousand.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: A unit with its own records; exchange measurable in money
Non-current and current; capital = assets − liabilities
Capital: lasting benefit; revenue: current year
Trade not recorded; cash recorded; net purchases and sales; opening and closing stock

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: basic accounting terms

slides.narration: In short. An entity keeps its own records. A transaction is an exchange measurable in money. Capital equals assets minus liabilities, and drawings reduce it. Expenditure is capital or revenue. Profit is income minus expenses. Trade discount is not recorded but cash discount is. Net figures are found after returns.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 2

rows: Drawings are a withdrawal and reduce capital
Trade discount is entered in the books
Only the net invoice amount is entered
Cash discount is calculated on the list price
It is calculated on the invoice amount
Repairs that only maintain an asset are revenue expenditure

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in Part 2 and what to write instead

slides.narration: Never call drawings an expense. Remember that only the net invoice amount is entered when trade discount is given. Work out cash discount on the invoice amount. Show the working for capital as assets minus liabilities. Give an example with each definition.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning of accounting; book-keeping; branches
sections.body_md:
**Accounting** is a process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and interpreting financial information and communicating it to users. Classical definitions describe it as the art of recording, classifying and summarising in money terms the transactions of a business, and of interpreting the results. It is an **information system**.

**Book-keeping** covers only the recording and classifying stages. Accounting uses those records and goes further.

**Branches:** financial accounting (the whole business, for outsiders), cost accounting (the cost of products and jobs) and management accounting (information for planning and control).

key_terms.definition_md: The process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing, interpreting and communicating financial information to users.
The recording and classifying of transactions in the books of account.
The branch that records the transactions of the whole business and reports its profit and financial position.
The branch that finds and analyses the cost of products, jobs and services.
The branch that presents information to managers for planning, control and decisions.

sections.heading: 2. Objectives and role of accounting
sections.body_md:
**Objectives:** a systematic record of transactions; the profit or loss of a period; the financial position on a date; information to users.

**Role:** language of business; historical record; current economic reality; information system; service to users.

Accounting cannot guarantee a profit. It measures and reports what has happened.

rows: Every transaction is written in an orderly way
Dhanpur Dairy notes each milk purchase and sale by date
Income of the period is compared with its expenses
The dairy compares a month of sales with a month of costs
Assets, liabilities and capital are shown on a date
The dairy lists what it owns and owes on 31 March
Figures reach those who must decide
The dairy gives its bank the year's statements

Each user gets the figures needed for a decision

sections.heading: 3. Users of accounting information
sections.body_md:
**Internal users** are inside the firm: owners (profit, safety of capital), management (detailed facts for decisions) and employees (wages, bonus, job security).

**External users** are outside it: banks and lenders (ability to repay), investors (return and risk), suppliers and creditors (ability to pay), government and tax authorities (profit for tax), consumers (price and supply) and researchers (facts for study).

key_terms.definition_md: Users who own, manage or work in the business.
Users outside the business, such as lenders, investors, suppliers, tax authorities, consumers and researchers.

sections.heading: 4. Qualitative characteristics of accounting information
sections.body_md:
- **Reliability:** verifiable (independent persons reach the same figure), neutral (free from bias), a faithful representation (describes what really happened).
- **Relevance:** timely (in time for the decision), with predictive value (helps forecast) and feedback value (confirms or corrects expectations).
- **Understandability:** clear to users with reasonable knowledge.
- **Comparability:** across periods (same methods, changes disclosed) and across firms.

key_terms.definition_md: The quality that lets independent persons using the same evidence reach the same figure.
Freedom of information from bias in favour of any user.
The availability of information in time to influence a decision.
The ability to compare information across periods and across firms.

sections.heading: 5. Basic terms: entity, transaction, capital, drawings, assets, liabilities
sections.body_md:
An **entity** is a person or organisation about which records are kept. A **business transaction** is an exchange of money or money's worth that can be measured in money. **Capital** is the owner's investment together with profits kept in the firm; **drawings** are cash or goods taken out for personal use and reduce capital.

**Capital = assets − liabilities.** For Meera Traders (imagined): assets ₹7,70,000 less liabilities ₹2,70,000 gives capital ₹5,00,000.

Assets are **non-current** (tangible or intangible) or **current**; liabilities are **non-current** (due after twelve months) or **current**.

key_terms.definition_md: A person or organisation with a separate existence for which records are kept.
An exchange of money or money's worth between the firm and another party, measurable in money.
The amount invested by the owner in the business, with profits left in it.
Cash or goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use.
A resource owned by the firm from which future benefit is expected.
An amount the firm is obliged to pay to outsiders.
A non-current asset without physical form that has value, such as a patent or goodwill.

sections.heading: 6. Expenditure, expense, income, profit, gain and loss
sections.body_md:
**Capital expenditure** gives a benefit lasting more than a year or adds to an asset (a van, installing a machine) and goes to the balance sheet. **Revenue expenditure** is used up within the year (wages, repairs) and is charged to the profit and loss account.

An **expense** is a cost incurred to earn revenue; **income** is what the firm earns; **profit** = income − expenses (Kaveri Bakery: ₹1,85,000 − ₹1,45,000 = ₹40,000). A **gain** comes from an incidental event (₹3,000 on selling an old computer above book value); a **loss** is a fall in capital with no benefit in return.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that book-keeping includes interpretation: it covers recording and classifying only.
- Treating drawings as an expense: they reduce capital.
- Entering trade discount in the books: only the net invoice amount is entered.
- Calculating cash discount on the list price: it is on the invoice amount.
- Calling repairs capital expenditure: repairs that only maintain an asset are revenue expenditure.

**Tips:** write the stages of the process in a definition; name the user and what the user needs; show assets minus liabilities as working for capital; give an example with each definition; split a classification question into one line per item.

Preparing a list of ledger balances to see whether the books agree
Finding the tax a business has to pay at the end of the year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing, interpreting and communicating financial information to its users. Accounting begins with identifying events that can be expressed in money and ends with communicating the results. Writing transactions in order is only recording, the list of balances is a test of arithmetic accuracy, and tax is one use of the information, not the whole process.

questions.stem_md: At Dhanpur Dairy (an imagined firm), a clerk records every sale and purchase, while the accountant also studies why the margin fell this quarter and explains it to the owner. Which activity belongs to accounting but not to book-keeping?

options.text_md: Entering the milk purchases under the right heads
Noting a cheque received from a shop
Studying and explaining the fall in the margin

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Studying and explaining the fall in the margin. Book-keeping is limited to recording and classifying transactions. Analysing results and explaining them to a user is part of the wider function of accounting. The other three are routine recording tasks.

questions.stem_md: Zenith Pens (an imagined firm) wants to know exactly how much it spends to make one pen of each model, so that it can fix selling prices. Which branch of accounting supplies this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Cost accounting. Cost accounting collects and analyses the cost of producing a unit or a job. Financial accounting reports the whole business for outside users, and the other two serve different purposes.

questions.stem_md: The branch of accounting that supplies information to managers for planning, controlling and decision making is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** management accounting. Management accounting is designed for internal managers. Financial accounting prepares general-purpose statements for outsiders, book-keeping only records, and auditing is an independent check of the accounts.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT an objective of accounting?

options.text_md: Keeping a systematic record of transactions
Finding the profit or loss of an accounting period
Guaranteeing that the business will earn a profit every year
Showing the financial position on a given date

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Guaranteeing that the business will earn a profit every year. Accounting measures and reports results; it cannot guarantee them. The other three are the standard objectives: systematic records, ascertaining profit or loss, and depicting financial position.

questions.stem_md: Tara Tailors (an imagined firm) applies for a loan. Before sanctioning it, the bank studies her accounts. What is the bank mainly trying to learn?

options.text_md: Whether the firm will be able to pay interest and repay the loan
How much bonus the employees should get
Whether the firm's goods are priced fairly for consumers
How the firm's profit compares with that of other trades in the country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Whether the firm will be able to pay interest and repay the loan. A lender is concerned with safety of its money, so it looks at liquidity and the ability to service the debt. Bonus is an employee concern, price fairness a consumer concern, and an industry comparison a researcher's concern.

questions.stem_md: An income tax officer asks Ravi Agencies (an imagined firm) for its books. For which purpose does the officer need the accounting information?

options.text_md: To decide whether to supply goods on credit
To judge whether the owner deserves a salary increase
To compare the firm's prices with those of rivals
To work out the profit on which tax is payable

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To work out the profit on which tax is payable. Government and tax authorities use accounts to assess taxable income and to check compliance. Supplier credit is a creditor's concern, and the remaining two are not tax matters.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an internal user of accounting information?

options.text_md: The bank that gave a loan

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The manager of the firm. Internal users work in or own the business: owners, managers and employees. Suppliers, banks and researchers sit outside the firm and are external users.

questions.stem_md: When it is said that accounting provides a permanent record of what the firm did in the past, which role of accounting is being described?

options.text_md: A substitute for the owner's own judgement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A historical record of transactions. Accounting stores past transactions so that they can be looked up, verified and compared. Forecasting uses the record but is not the record itself, accounting does not replace judgement, and records do not guarantee that fraud cannot occur.

questions.stem_md: Nikhil is thinking of putting savings into a growing imagined bakery chain. From its accounts he wants to know chiefly

options.text_md: how much customers saved through discounts
how profitable the chain is and how safe his investment would be
what rent the chain pays to each landlord
how many of the staff are paid on time

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** how profitable the chain is and how safe his investment would be. An investor looks for returns and risk, which the profit and financial position reveal. The other items are not what a prospective investor mainly seeks from the accounts.

questions.stem_md: The sales figures of Orchid Stores (an imagined firm) for March reach the owner only in the middle of June, after she has already placed the next season's orders. Which quality of accounting information is missing?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Timeliness, a part of relevance. Information that arrives after the decision is made cannot influence it, so it lacks timeliness. Nothing in the case questions the clarity of the report, the fairness of the reporter or whether the figures can be checked.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of Pinewood Traders (an imagined firm) leaves out some bad debts from the report so that the owner is pleased. Which characteristic has been violated?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Neutrality. Neutral information is free from bias and is not coloured to please a user. Leaving out unpleasant facts to please the owner is a failure of neutrality. The other characteristics are not the issue.

questions.stem_md: Two accountants separately examine the invoices and receipts of the same imagined firm and arrive at the same sales figure. This shows that the information is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** verifiable. Verifiability means independent persons using the same evidence reach the same result. Comparability concerns similarity across periods or firms, and predictive value and timeliness concern usefulness for decisions.

questions.stem_md: Sunrise Garments (an imagined firm) valued its closing stock by one method in 2023, a second in 2024 and a third in 2025, without saying so. What is the main problem for a reader comparing the three years?

options.text_md: The information has no predictive value because it is about the past
The report is too technical to be understood
The results of the three years are not comparable
The statements are not verifiable by an auditor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The results of the three years are not comparable. Changing the method every year makes the yearly figures differ for reasons that have nothing to do with performance, so they cannot be compared. Predictive value and verifiability are about different things, and nothing says the report is technical.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of an imagined village cooperative adds short notes in plain words under each statement so that members with little schooling can follow them. This supports
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** understandability. Information should be presented so that users with reasonable knowledge can follow it. Plain notes serve this directly. They do not by themselves make figures reliable, comparable across firms or earlier.

questions.stem_md: Information that helps users forecast what is likely to happen in the future has
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** predictive value. Predictive value is the ability to help users make forecasts. Feedback value confirms or corrects earlier expectations, and the other two belong to reliability.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a business transaction of Gopal Garments (an imagined firm)?

options.text_md: A customer asking the price of a shirt
The owner's family going on a picnic
The owner thinking of opening a new branch next year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Paying ₹7,000 for the shop rent. A business transaction is an exchange of money or money's worth between the firm and another party that can be measured in money. Paying rent qualifies. An enquiry, the owner's family outing and a mere plan involve no completed exchange of the firm's resources.

questions.stem_md: The amount which the proprietor has invested in the business, together with profits left in it, is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** capital. Capital is the owner's claim on the firm. Drawings are amounts taken out, liabilities are owed to outsiders and revenue is income from the main activity.

questions.stem_md: Mohan, who owns an imagined provision store, takes goods costing ₹2,000 from the shop for use in his own kitchen. This is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** drawings. Goods taken by the owner for personal use are drawings and reduce his capital. They are not bought for the business, are not a cost of running it and are not a loss from an adverse event.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a current liability?

options.text_md: Bank loan repayable after five years
Creditors for goods bought on credit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Creditors for goods bought on credit. Creditors are to be paid within the operating cycle or one year. A five-year loan is non-current, capital is owner's equity and furniture is an asset.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an intangible asset?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Patent rights. An intangible asset has no physical form but has value, as a patent does. A computer is a tangible non-current asset, and stock and bank balance are current assets.

questions.stem_md: Kaveri Bakery (an imagined firm) spent ₹4,50,000 on a delivery van and ₹3,000 on repairing its oven. Which treatment is correct?

options.text_md: The van is capital expenditure and the repair is revenue expenditure
The van is revenue expenditure and the repair is capital expenditure

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The van is capital expenditure and the repair is revenue expenditure. The van will serve for several years, so the spending gives a lasting benefit and is capital. Repairs only keep the oven in working order, so they are revenue. The other options reverse or merge the two.

questions.stem_md: An old computer in the books of an imagined coaching centre at ₹12,000 is sold for ₹15,000. The ₹3,000 excess is best described as
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a gain. The amount comes from an incidental transaction, not from the centre's regular teaching business, and it exceeds the book value, so it is a gain. It is not an expense or drawings, and not revenue from the main activity.

questions.stem_md: A deduction given by a wholesaler from the catalogue price when a retailer buys in large quantity is

options.text_md: cash discount, which is entered in the books
trade discount, which is not entered in the books
trade discount, which is entered as an expense
cash discount, which is not entered in the books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** trade discount, which is not entered in the books. Trade discount is given on the list price at the time of sale and only the net invoice price is recorded. Cash discount is for prompt payment and is recorded in the books.

questions.stem_md: A written document that supports an entry and serves as proof of a transaction, such as a cash memo, is called a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** voucher. A voucher is documentary evidence of a transaction. A ledger is a book of accounts, while a trial balance and a balance sheet are statements prepared from the books.

questions.stem_md: Closing stock of ₹31,000 at 31 March of an imagined stationery shop will, on 1 April, be

options.text_md: opening stock of the new year
a liability of the new year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** opening stock of the new year. The goods left unsold at the end of one period are carried forward and form the opening stock of the next period. They are not new purchases, and they are an asset, not a liability or drawings.

questions.stem_md: A person who owes money to the firm for goods bought on credit is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** debtor. A debtor owes the firm, so the amount is an asset. A creditor is owed by the firm. A proprietor is the owner and a drawer is the person who draws a bill or cheque.

questions.stem_md: During one year an imagined shop sold goods for ₹2,40,000, of which customers returned goods worth ₹15,000. Its net sales for the year are
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹2,25,000. Net sales equal sales minus sales returns, so ₹2,40,000 less ₹15,000 gives ₹2,25,000. Adding the returns, using the returns alone or ignoring them gives the other figures.

questions.stem_md: A fire destroys goods worth ₹40,000 in the godown of an imagined firm, and nothing is recovered. This amount is

options.text_md: an expense, because it was incurred to earn revenue
drawings, because it reduces the owner's capital
a gain, because the goods are no longer held
a loss, because it is a fall in capital without any benefit in return

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a loss, because it is a fall in capital without any benefit in return. A loss is a reduction in the owner's claim from an unplanned event, with nothing received in exchange. An expense is a cost of earning income, drawings are withdrawals by the owner, and the destruction of goods is not a gain.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Accounting is called an information system.

**Reason (R):** It collects data about transactions, processes them into statements and communicates the results to those who need them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. The three steps in R, collect, process and communicate, are exactly what makes accounting an information system.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Accounting has a wider scope than book-keeping.

**Reason (R):** Book-keeping includes the analysis and interpretation of the recorded results.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true because accounting goes on to summarise, analyse and interpret. R is false: book-keeping stops at recording and classifying, and analysis and interpretation belong to accounting.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A bank that has lent money to a firm is an external user of its accounts.

**Reason (R):** A lender wants to know whether the firm can pay the interest and repay the loan.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R states what the bank needs, not why it is external. The bank is external because it is not part of the firm's ownership or management.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Information supported by bills and receipts is considered more reliable.

**Reason (R):** Independent persons who look at the same bills and receipts would reach much the same figures.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. R is the idea of verifiability, and it is the reason supporting documents raise reliability.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Drawings reduce the capital of the owner.

**Reason (R):** Drawings are an expense of the business and are charged against its profit.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true because the owner has taken part of his claim out. R is false: drawings are a private withdrawal, not a business expense, and they are not charged against profit.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Profit on the sale of an old machine is treated as a gain and not as revenue.

**Reason (R):** Such a profit does not arise from the normal activity of the business.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Revenue arises from the main activity, so a profit from an incidental sale is classed as a gain, and R gives that reason.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A bank loan repayable after four years is a current liability.

**Reason (R):** Liabilities that are due for payment after more than twelve months are non-current liabilities.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the loan is not due within twelve months, so it is non-current. R is true and is the very test that places the loan in the non-current group.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Book-keeping includes interpreting the final results for the use of management.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Interpreting results belongs to accounting. Book-keeping is confined to recording and classifying transactions.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cash discount is allowed to a debtor for paying within the agreed period and is recorded in the books.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Cash discount rewards prompt payment. The seller books it as a discount allowed and the buyer as a discount received.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The closing stock of one accounting year is the opening stock of the next year.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The unsold goods are carried forward at the same value into the new period.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Goodwill of ₹50,000 in the list of Meera Traders (an imagined stationery business) is a tangible non-current asset.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Goodwill has no physical form, so it is an intangible non-current asset. Furniture or a computer would be tangible.

questions.stem_md: The part of accounting that is concerned only with recording transactions is called ___.
questions.solution_md: It is book-keeping; accounting goes on to summarise, analyse and communicate.

questions.stem_md: A deduction from the list price given by a seller for buying in bulk is called ___ discount.
questions.solution_md: It is trade discount, and it does not appear in the books.

questions.stem_md: Cash taken out of the business by the owner for private use is recorded as ___, which reduces ___.
questions.solution_md: The amount is drawings, and it reduces capital.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined user of the accounts of a small tea company with what that user mainly wants from them.

options.text_md: A bank that lent money to the company
A supplier selling tea leaves on credit

match_right.text_md: Whether the firm can pay its dues on time
Capacity to pay wages and bonus
Ability to pay interest and repay the loan
Profit on which tax is payable

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each user looks at the accounts for the information that bears on its own decision.

questions.stem_md: Match each item in the books of an imagined stationery shop with the term that describes it.

options.text_md: A customer who has not yet paid for pens sold on credit
A paper mill to which the shop owes money
Pens received back from a customer
Reams of paper unsold on the last day of the year

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). A person owing the firm is a debtor, a person owed is a creditor, goods sent back by a customer are a sales return, and the unsold goods at year end are closing stock.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these stages of the accounting process in the order in which they take place.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (d) → (c) → (a). Transactions are first recorded, then classified, then summarised into statements, after which the results are interpreted and communicated.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps for finding what Hiral Electronics (an imagined firm) pays on a bill that has both discounts.

options.text_md: Deduct cash discount on the invoice amount

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (a) → (d) → (c) → (b). Cash discount is calculated on the invoice amount after trade discount, so the trade discount must be deducted first.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Meera Traders (an imagined stationery business in the imagined town of Ranipur) has these balances: land and building ₹4,00,000, furniture ₹60,000, computer ₹40,000, goodwill ₹50,000, stock ₹80,000, debtors ₹70,000, cash in hand ₹30,000, cash at bank ₹40,000, bank loan ₹2,00,000, creditors ₹60,000 and outstanding rent ₹10,000. Find the owner's capital in rupees.
questions.solution_md: Assets total ₹7,70,000 and liabilities total ₹2,70,000, so capital is assets minus liabilities, ₹5,00,000.

questions.stem_md: In a year, Meera Traders bought goods for cash ₹60,000 and on credit ₹90,000, and returned goods worth ₹12,000 to a supplier. Find the net purchases in rupees.
questions.solution_md: Purchases are ₹1,50,000 and purchases return is ₹12,000, so net purchases are ₹1,38,000.

questions.stem_md: Anand Sports (an imagined wholesaler) sells goods to a retailer at a list price of ₹50,000 and allows trade discount at 10%. Find the trade discount in rupees.

Kiran Stores (an imagined retailer) buys goods listed at ₹80,000 and gets trade discount at 15%. The seller also allows cash discount at 5% on the invoice amount if payment is made within ten days, and Kiran Stores pays in time. How much does it pay, in rupees?
questions.solution_md: Trade discount ₹12,000 gives an invoice of ₹68,000. Cash discount at 5% on that is ₹3,400, so the payment is ₹64,600.

questions.stem_md: In one month Kaveri Bakery (an imagined firm in the imagined town of Dhanpur) earned ₹1,80,000 from sale of cakes and bread and ₹5,000 as commission. It spent ₹95,000 on flour, sugar and butter used, ₹30,000 on wages, ₹12,000 on rent and ₹8,000 on electricity. Find the profit for the month in rupees.
questions.solution_md: Income is ₹1,85,000 and expenses are ₹1,45,000, so profit is ₹40,000.

questions.stem_md: Meera Traders sold goods worth ₹18,000 on credit to Rohit Stationers (an imagined shop). Rohit later paid ₹6,000 on account. How much does he still owe, in rupees?
questions.solution_md: He bought for ₹18,000 and paid ₹6,000, so the balance due from this debtor is ₹12,000.

questions.stem_md: Define accounting and state why it is called an information system.
questions.solution_md: Give the standard definition and link it to collecting, processing and communicating.

answer.model_answer_md: Accounting is the art of **recording, classifying and summarising** money-related transactions and **interpreting** the results. It is an **information system** because it collects data about transactions, processes it into statements and **communicates** it to users who need it for decisions.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between book-keeping and accounting.
questions.solution_md: Contrast scope and purpose.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Scope:** book-keeping only **records and classifies** transactions; accounting also **summarises, analyses and interprets** them.
2. **Users and purpose:** book-keeping supplies the basic data, usually handled by a clerk; accounting uses it to give **information and advice** to management and others.

questions.stem_md: State any four objectives of accounting.
questions.solution_md: Any four of the standard objectives, half a mark each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Keeping a **systematic record** of transactions.
2. Finding the **profit or loss** of a period.
3. Showing the **financial position** on a date.
4. Providing **information to users** for decisions.

questions.stem_md: Why is accounting called the language of business? Explain briefly.
questions.solution_md: Link the idea of a language with communication of financial facts.

answer.model_answer_md: A language carries messages between people. Accounting turns the many events of a business into **money terms and standard statements** that owners, lenders, tax officers and others can read. In this way it **communicates** how the business is doing to everyone who has a stake in it.

marking_scheme.step: A language communicates; accounting communicates financial facts
Standard statements read by many users

questions.stem_md: Distinguish internal users from external users of accounting information, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Define each group and give one example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Internal users** are those inside the business who run or own it and use detailed information to manage it, for example the **manager**. **External users** are outside parties who deal with the business and rely on its published statements, for example a **bank** that has given a loan.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined bakeries, Anita Bakes and Latif Bakes, value their closing stock by different methods, and Anita also changed her method this year. Explain how this affects comparability.
questions.solution_md: Comparability across firms and across periods is both affected.

answer.model_answer_md: Comparability needs **similar methods** across firms and over time. Because Anita and Latif use different methods, their profits **cannot be compared fairly**. Anita's change means her own profits for the two years are **not comparable** either, unless the effect is disclosed.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish capital from drawings in two points.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, and effect on the owner's claim.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Capital** is the owner's investment plus profits left in the firm; **drawings** are cash or goods the owner takes out for private use.
2. Capital is the **owner's claim** on the firm; drawings **reduce** that claim and are not a business expense.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish trade discount from cash discount in two points.
questions.solution_md: Reason for giving, and treatment in the books.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Trade discount** is allowed on the list price for bulk buying or to a trader; **cash discount** is allowed for payment within the agreed period.
2. Trade discount is **not recorded** in the books, only the net invoice amount; cash discount is **recorded** as a discount allowed or received.

marking_scheme.step: Basis on which each is allowed

questions.stem_md: Rent of ₹12,000 paid by Kaveri Bakery is an expense, while ₹40,000 of goods destroyed by fire is a loss. Explain the difference between the two items.
questions.solution_md: An expense helps to earn revenue; a loss does not.

answer.model_answer_md: Rent is a **cost incurred to earn revenue**: the shop is used to make sales, so it is matched against income. Goods destroyed by fire are an **unplanned fall in the owner's claim** which earns **no revenue** in exchange, so it is a loss.

questions.stem_md: Classify each of these items of an imagined firm as a current asset, non-current asset, current liability or non-current liability: (Delivery van), (Wages payable to staff), (Amount due from a customer), (Loan repayable in four years).
questions.solution_md: Half a mark for each classification.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Delivery van: **non-current asset**.
2. Wages payable to staff: **current liability**.
3. Amount due from a customer: **current asset**.
4. Loan repayable in four years: **non-current liability**.

questions.stem_md: Kaveri Bakery (an imagined firm) has a bank loan, buys flour from a supplier on credit and employs six bakers. State what each of the three parties mainly wants from its accounts.
questions.solution_md: Each party looks at liquidity, solvency or profitability from its own viewpoint.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **bank** wants to know whether the bakery can pay interest and **repay the loan** on time.
2. The **flour supplier** wants to know whether the bakery can **pay its dues** so that credit can safely continue.
3. The **bakers** want to know whether the bakery earns enough to pay **wages and bonus** regularly and stay in business.

questions.stem_md: Name the quality of accounting information that is weak in each case of an imagined firm: (i) the owner tells the accountant to show a higher profit than the books support; (ii) the annual report is written in such complex language that the shareholders cannot follow it; (iii) the report on the cost of an order reaches the manager after the order is completed.
questions.solution_md: Match each case to bias, clarity and time.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Neutrality** (part of reliability): information must be free from bias; the owner's pressure makes the profit a distortion.
2. **Understandability**: a report that its users cannot follow does not help them.
3. **Timeliness** (part of relevance): information that arrives after the decision is of no use to the manager.

questions.stem_md: Classify the following items of Tinku Toys (an imagined firm) under the correct head: (1) A patent bought by a toy firm; (2) A packing machine; (3) Unsold toys in the godown; (4) Amount due from a toy shop; (5) Rent unpaid for March; (6) A loan from a bank for six years.
questions.solution_md: Half a mark for each correct classification.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A patent bought by a toy firm: **Non-current asset (intangible)**.
2. A packing machine: **Non-current asset (tangible)**.
3. Unsold toys in the godown: **Current asset**.
4. Amount due from a toy shop: **Current asset (debtors)**.
5. Rent unpaid for March: **Current liability**.
6. A loan from a bank for six years: **Non-current liability**.

questions.stem_md: Vikram Cycles (an imagined firm) has assets: furniture ₹90,000, stock ₹60,000, debtors ₹50,000 and cash ₹20,000. Its liabilities are creditors ₹45,000 and a bank loan ₹75,000. questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning of accounting and discuss its objectives.
questions.solution_md: Definition with the stages, then the four standard objectives with a line each.

answer.model_answer_md:
Accounting is a process of **identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and interpreting** financial information, and **communicating** it to users for decisions. It is the system through which a business reports on itself.

**Objectives:**
1. **Systematic records:** to keep complete and orderly records of all transactions so that nothing is missed.
2. **Profit or loss:** to find the result of operations for the period by comparing income with expenses.
3. **Financial position:** to show assets, liabilities and capital on a particular date.
4. **Information to users:** to supply owners, managers, lenders and others with the figures they need.

questions.stem_md: Explain, with the needs of each, any five users of accounting information, including at least two internal users.
questions.solution_md: Five users, one mark each, at least two internal.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Internal users**
1. **Owners:** want to know profit earned and the safety of their capital.
2. **Management:** needs detailed figures to plan, control and decide.
3. **Employees:** want to know whether the firm can pay wages and bonus and offer secure jobs.

**External users**
4. **Banks and lenders:** need the ability to pay interest and repay loans.
5. **Suppliers and creditors:** want to know whether the firm can pay for goods bought on credit.
6. **Tax authorities:** need the profit for assessing tax.
7. **Investors, consumers and researchers** use the accounts to judge returns, price fairness and trends respectively.

(Any five, one mark each.)

questions.stem_md: Explain reliability, relevance, understandability and comparability, using one imagined example for each.
questions.solution_md: Four characteristics with their parts and an example each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Reliability:** information is **verifiable, neutral** and **faithful to the facts**. Example: a sales figure backed by invoices that two auditors both confirm.
2. **Relevance:** it has **predictive and feedback value** and arrives in **time**. Example: a weekly cost report that lets a baker change prices before a festival.
3. **Understandability:** it is presented so that users with reasonable knowledge can follow it. Example: plain labels and notes on a statement for cooperative members.
4. **Comparability:** it can be compared **across periods and across firms** because the same methods are used. Example: two shops using the same stock valuation method for five years.

questions.stem_md: Explain how assets and liabilities are classified, giving an example of each class.
questions.solution_md: Two classes of assets with the tangible and intangible split, and two classes of liabilities, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Assets** are resources owned by the firm that give future benefit.
1. **Non-current assets** serve for more than one year. They are **tangible** (land, machinery) or **intangible** (patents, goodwill).
2. **Current assets** are expected to turn into cash within a year or the operating cycle: stock, debtors, cash.

**Liabilities** are amounts the firm must pay to outsiders.
3. **Non-current liabilities** fall due after more than a year, for example a long-term loan.
4. **Current liabilities** are due within a year, for example creditors and outstanding expenses.

Assets are financed by liabilities and capital.

questions.stem_md: Kaveri Bakery (an imagined firm) made these payments in a month: (1) Buying a delivery van for ₹4,50,000; (2) Painting the shop walls, done every year, ₹8,000; (3) Repairs to the oven, ₹3,000; (4) Paying ₹12,000 to install and fix a new mixing machine; (5) Buying flour for the month, ₹30,000; (6) Buying a display counter for ₹35,000. Classify each as capital or revenue expenditure and say what would happen to the profit if the bakery wrongly treated the capital items as revenue expenditure.
questions.solution_md: Lasting benefit means capital; recurring, upkeep and consumed items are revenue; mixing them up distorts profit and asset values.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Buying a delivery van for ₹4,50,000: **Capital**.
2. Painting the shop walls, done every year, ₹8,000: **Revenue**.
3. Repairs to the oven, ₹3,000: **Revenue**.
4. Paying ₹12,000 to install and fix a new mixing machine: **Capital**.
5. Buying flour for the month, ₹30,000: **Revenue**.
6. Buying a display counter for ₹35,000: **Capital**.

Capital items total ₹4,97,000 and revenue items ₹41,000. Charging the capital items to the profit and loss account would **understate profit** by ₹4,97,000 and show the assets too low, because the vans, machines and counters are meant to serve for years.
